Engagement with Muslims did improve under Keir Starmer's Labour government, but the relationship remained fraught: large numbers of Muslim voters abandoned Labour over its support for Israel during the Gaza genocide.

Morocco’s King Mohammed VI has appointed Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri as head of the government, one week after her party won the legislative elections.
For the first time in its history, the North African kingdom will be led by a woman.
“This is truly a historic moment,” El Mansouri told public media after her audience at the royal palace.
“For the first time in our country’s history, a woman is taking on the responsibility of leading the government. This is not only a source of pride for me, but for all Moroccan women,” she added.
At 50, the lawyer becomes the thrid woman in the Arab world to reach this position, after Najla Bouden and Sarra Zaafarani in Tunisia.
El Mansouri had already made history by becoming, at just 33, the first woman to serve as mayor of the tourist city of Marrakesh in 2009 - a position she currently holds for a second term since 2021.
She had also made her mark during the 2023 earthquake, visiting affected communities repeatedly.
Currently the national coordinator of the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), outgoing minister of housing and spatial planning, and a newly re-elected MP, El Mansouri had been widely tipped for the role in recent weeks.
However, without an absolute majority, the new prime minister will now need to form a coalition government for the next five years ahead of the 9 October parliamentary session.

A 72-hour-old newborn is laid to sleep on a thin, worn-out mattress on the floor of a school in Sidon, south Lebanon, his first days unfolding in a classroom-turned-shelter.
His mother, Hala Loubany, 29, has just had a C-section. She watches over the baby boy, one hand resting protectively over the throbbing scar on her stomach.
Next to them, separated by a shelf crammed with canned food and clothes, an elderly man is preparing lunch for himself and his wife.
Three families live in this classroom, their few belongings packed into corners as they wait to return to Nabatieh’s southern district.
Israel's bombardment has destroyed infrastructure, including thousands of homes, across south Lebanon, with more than two dozen Lebanese border towns and villages razed. Tens of thousands of people have been displaced.
“Hala’s water broke here, in the school, so she was taken to the hospital at the last minute,” her father, Ali Mahmoud Loubany, told Middle East Eye. “It was an emergency so doctors performed a C-section.”
Hala was six months pregnant when she, her husband, their two sons, aged six and one, and her father fled Nabatieh. The school in Sidon is the second shelter they have been forced to seek refuge in.
Directly opposite the classroom is the only women’s bathroom on the floor. Families have to schedule showers in the three laminate stalls and wash their clothes in the shallow sinks.
For Hala, who is still recovering from surgery, poor sanitation is a major source of anxiety, as she worries about her wound becoming infected.
'No one by our side'
At 54, her father says he is “sick” of his family being displaced

When Grand Ayatollah Mousa Shobeiri Zanjani died at 98 on 20 September, he left behind a rare position in Iran’s religious establishment: a cleric who kept his distance from political power, yet whose influence reached across the Islamic Republic’s deepest political divides.
His students included former reformist President Mohammad Khatami and, according to a source in the Qom Seminary, Mojtaba Khamenei, the current supreme leader. For decades, politicians and clerics on opposing sides of Iran’s political spectrum turned to Shobeiri because his authority rested outside politics.
That independence made him an important figure at moments when Iran’s political and religious establishments collided.
Shobeiri was one of seven senior clerics identified by the Society of Seminary Scholars of Qom in the 1990s as qualified to be followed as a grand ayatollah and serve as a marja, or religious authority.
The ayatollah belonged to a strand of the Iranian clergy that believed clerics should not directly enter politics.
They are often described as “traditional” clerics, a group that includes Ayatollah Vahid Khorasani, another highly respected figure in the seminary establishment. Both men have largely stayed outside of the Islamic Republic's factional politics.
Traditional clerics tend to see their role primarily as preserving the independence of the seminaries from the state, maintaining the institution of marjaʿiyyah – the system of senior religious authorities whom believers may follow for guidance on matters of Islamic law – and addressing religious and social affairs rather than directly participating in political power.

A narrow choke point that normally handles a fifth of the world's daily oil supply, as well as a fifth of globally traded liquefied natural gas, sits almost silent under the watch of multibillion-dollar American warships that cannot convince commercial insurers to risk even a handful of tankers.
Washington can still destroy almost anything it targets across the Middle East, but whether that destruction can buy the political outcome it wants is a vastly different question.

On
A rapid offensive by Yemen’s Houthis has intensified the country’s civil war and caused chaos in global oil markets.
The group, which has controlled much of northern Yemen for over a decade, has seized fresh territory from the pro-government forces and threatened shipping traffic, notably that of Saudi Arabia, in the Bab el-Mandeb strait, the maritime chokepoint linking the Gulf of Aden to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.
With few signs of military formality, the group has often been described in international media as a "ragtag fighting force".
But over the past two decades, the Houthis have evolved to use missiles and drones to stage attacks inside Yemen as well as against Israel, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others.
Much of the group’s arsenal has either been designed or supplied by Iran, which regards the force as a member of its Axis of Resistance, a network of allies that also includes Hamas and Hezbollah.
The Houthis have also acquired weapons, including decades-old Soviet-era tanks and helicopters, after victory on the battlefield, and recently seized US-supplied military vehicles captured from retreating Saudi-backed forces.
While the Houthis’ stockpile levels are unknown, it is possible to assemble a sense of their firepower and military capabilities.

The most prominent political casualty so far has been Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy head of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and family minister from 2016 to 2018. She resigned on Sunday after the opposition accused her of making substantial profits from share sales shortly before the funds crisis triggered a major stock market sell-off on 16 September.
Erdogan addressed the controversy on Monday, pledging to pursue those responsible for market manipulation and fraudulent trading schemes.
“Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets or legal interests will face us and the state,” he said.
The funds in question concentrated their holdings in illiquid stocks with low free floats, making their prices easier to inflate because relatively few shares were available for trading. For example, the Tera investment fund generated a return of over 1,500 percent over the past year, a figure that is totally illogical by any market calculation or method.

In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel. It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a "substantial risk" of contributing to what it calls Israel's "ongoing genocide".
The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets.
A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians, including a young man who may lose his vision forever.
The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there.
India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Israeli forces have stepped up restrictions on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank during the Jewish holiday of Sukkot, blocking roads, limiting movement and causing hours-long waits at checkpoints.
The army has blocked entrances to several towns and villages with iron gates and earth mounds, including on secondary roads, since the Jewish holiday of Sukkot began on 25 September.
Checkpoints have also been tightened across the territory, as a comprehensive closure of the West Bank is set to remain in place until the holiday ends on 3 October.
The Atara and Ein Siniya checkpoints north of Ramallah, along with the Jaba’ checkpoint northeast of Jerusalem, stand out as prominent examples of checkpoints characterised by long waiting times, particularly during peak hours.
These checkpoints slow the movement of Palestinians between villages, towns and cities, with delays often extending further depending on inspection procedures and conditions at the site, thereby creating major bottlenecks on routes used daily by thousands of Palestinians.
